title: Israel Asks for a King
overview: Israel's leaders ask Samuel for a king so they can be like the nations around them, and God allows it while warning them what a king will cost.

parts.label: Samuel's sons go wrong (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: In his old age Samuel made his two sons judges in Beersheba, in the far south, but they took bribes and twisted court rulings for money. Their corruption gave the people a real complaint.

parts.label: The elders want a king (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Until now Israel had no king; it was led by judges and prophets, and the LORD was seen as the nation's true ruler. The tribal leaders come to Samuel's home in Ramah and ask him to appoint a king, so they can have what the other nations have.

parts.label: God's reply to Samuel (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: Samuel is upset and prays, and God tells him the people are rejecting God as their king, not Samuel, continuing a pattern that goes back to leaving Egypt. Still, God tells Samuel to agree, but first to warn them plainly what a king will demand.

parts.label: What a king will take (vv. 10-18)
parts.note: Samuel describes how kings of that world usually behaved: drafting sons for the army and royal farms, putting daughters to work in the palace, seizing the best land, and claiming a tenth of crops and flocks. The word "take" keeps repeating, and the warning ends bleakly: one day they will cry out against the king they chose and find no relief.

parts.label: The people insist (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: The people refuse to listen and still want a king to rule them and lead them in battle, so they can be like other nations. God tells Samuel to give them one, and Samuel sends everyone back to their own towns.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether asking for a king was wrong in itself or only wrong in its motive and timing, since an earlier law (Deuteronomy 17) already allows for a king, and the surrounding chapters seem to hold both a critical and a more hopeful view of kingship.
think: When people trade some of their freedom for a strong leader who promises security, how can they tell whether the trade is worth it?
